Front:
RO feed SDI increases and MF TMP rises simultaneously. Why?
a. Higher solids loading in source water
b. Analyzer drift
c. Low ORP
d. UV fault
Back: Answer: a. Higher solids loading in source water

Front:
Sudden MF filtrate turbidity decrease without process change likely
indicates:
a. Improved performance
b. Analyzer dilution or flushing effect
c. Fiber break
d. CEB effectiveness
Back: Answer: b. Analyzer dilution or flushing effect

Front:
RO permeate flow decreases while concentrate flow increases.
Meaning?
a. Membrane breach
b. Recovery decrease (valve drift)
c. Fouling
d. Analyzer error
Back: Answer: b. Recovery decrease (valve drift)

Front:
RO feed pump trips intermittently on low suction pressure. Cause?
a. Analyzer drift
b. Scaling
c. Air entrainment or low NPSH
d. High recovery
Back: Answer: c. Air entrainment or low NPSH

Front:
UV system shows high apparent dose despite fouling. Why?
a. Sensor over-reading (miscalibration)
b. High UVT
c. Peroxide overfeed
d. Increased flow
Back: Answer: a. Sensor over-reading (miscalibration)

Front:
RO permeate conductivity spikes briefly after CEB or CIP.
Explanation?
a. Analyzer drift
b. Chemical cleaning causes temporary rejection loss
c. Scaling
d. Low pH
Back: Answer: b. Chemical cleaning causes temporary rejection loss

Front:
MF fouling increases rapidly following a raw water change. RO ΔP
also increases slightly. Why?
a. Higher solids loading from source water
b. Valve misalignment
c. Permeate blending error
d. High pH
Back: Answer: a. Higher solids loading from source water

Front:
RO feed pump trips frequently on low suction pressure. Most likely:
a. High ORP
b. Low NPSH or suction blockage
c. Analyzer drift
d. MF turbine fault
Back: Answer: b. Low NPSH or suction blockage

Front:
Sudden RO permeate conductivity spike coincides with cleaning. Why?
a. Analyzer drift
b. Chemical cleaning temporarily changes rejection
c. High pH
d. Scaling
Back: Answer: b. Chemical cleaning temporarily changes rejection

Front:
RO normalized flows vary widely between trains but pressures are
identical. Cause?
a. Instrument calibration drift
b. Scaling
c. Fouling
d. Cavitation
Back: Answer: a. Instrument calibration drift

Front:
MF filtrate turbidity drops after a storm. Interpretation?
a. Treatment improvements
b. Dilution effect or sample line flushing
c. Analyzer failure
d. Increased CEB frequency
Back: Answer: b. Dilution effect or sample line flushing

Front:
UV system shows high dose despite lamp age and low UVT. Why?
a. UV sensor calibration drift (reading artificially high)
b. High UVT
c. Peroxide overdose
d. Analyzer wiring failure
Back: Answer: a. UV sensor calibration drift (reading artificially high)

Front:
MF TMP increases and RO feed SDI increases at the same time. Likely
cause:
a. High solids loading from raw water
b. Biofilm in RO
c. Analyzer drift
d. Valve malfunction
Back: Answer: a. High solids loading from raw water

Front:
RO permeate conductivity spikes while ΔP is stable. Most likely:
a. Scaling
b. O-ring leak or membrane breach
c. Air entrainment
d. Analyzer turbidity error
Back: Answer: b. O-ring leak or membrane breach

Front:
Sudden drop in MF cycle time with normal TMP likely indicates:
a. Fouling
b. Flux too high
c. Backwash valve or cycle control issue
d. Analyzer drift
Back: Answer: c. Backwash valve or cycle control issue

Front:
RO pump trips on low suction pressure intermittently. Cause?
a. High ORP
b. Air entrainment or low NPSH
c. Scaling
d. High UVT
Back: Answer: b. Air entrainment or low NPSH

Front:
UV dose suddenly drops though UVT is high and lamps are near-new.
Cause?
a. Excess peroxide
b. UV sensor fouling or misalignment
c. Air scour issue
d. Concentrate valve drift
Back: Answer: b. UV sensor fouling or misalignment

Front:
After a storm event, MF filtrate turbidity increases but TMP
decreases. Why?
a. Membrane break
b. Analyzer dilution or inlet sample line flooded
c. Backwash failure
d. Concentrate valve stuck open
Back: Answer: b. Analyzer dilution or inlet sample line flooded

Front:
MF TMP increases and RO ΔP increases after a storm. Most likely
explanation:
a. Increased solids loading to MF and RO
b. Air entrainment
c. Antiscalant pump failure
d. Analyzer malfunction
Back: Answer: a. Increased solids loading to MF and RO

Front:
MF filtrate flow decreases but TMP stays constant. Why?
a. Flow meter error or calibration drift
b. Fouling
c. Scaling
d. Backwash failure
Back: Answer: a. Flow meter error or calibration drift

Front:
RO tail elements show declining permeate flow and higher
differential pressure. Most likely cause:
a. Biofouling in lead stage
b. Scaling in tail stage
c. Analyzer failure
d. Low ORP
Back: Answer: b. Scaling in tail stage

Front:
UV-AOP system shows low peroxide consumption and lower-than-expected
radical production. Cause?
a. Low pH
b. Peroxide underfeed
c. Lamp overdrive
d. High temperature
Back: Answer: b. Peroxide underfeed

Front:
A sudden RO permeate conductivity spike with normal ΔP indicates:
a. Membrane breach or o-ring seal failure
b. Scaling
c. Biofouling
d. Analyzer turbidity drift
Back: Answer: a. Membrane breach or o-ring seal failure

Front:
MF system cycles shorten dramatically without TMP change. Most
likely:
a. Scaling
b. High flux
c. Control valve or backwash valve malfunction
d. Low air scour
Back: Answer: c. Control valve or backwash valve malfunction

Front:
RO recovery drops without change in feed flow or pressure. Cause?
a. CIP needed
b. Membrane breach
c. Concentrate valve drifting toward open
d. High pH feed
Back: Answer: c. Concentrate valve drifting toward open

Front:
After a heavy rain event, MF TMP increases, RO feed SDI increases,
and RO ΔP begins trending upward. What is the best immediate
operational response?
a. Increase RO recovery to maintain permeate production
b. Reduce MF flux and increase the frequency of backwash/CEB cycles
c. Lower RO feed pressure to reduce ΔP
d. Increase antiscalant dose only
Back: Answer: b. Reduce MF flux and increase the frequency of backwash/CEB cycles

Front:
UV dose begins to fall short of setpoint despite full lamp power and
normal UVT. Operators recently increased RO recovery. How does this
indirectly impact UV-AOP?
a. Lower flow to the UV system, increasing dose
b. Higher permeate flow to UV, reducing hydraulic contact time
c. Lower permeate TDS, reducing UV absorbance
d. Incorrect UV setpoint in the SCADA system
Back: Answer: b. Higher permeate flow to UV, reducing hydraulic contact time

Front:
Two identical RO trains operate in parallel. Train A has a
significantly higher ΔP than Train B, but both produce similar
permeate quality and flow. What is the first troubleshooting step?
a. Immediately CIP both trains
b. Verify instrument calibration and check all valve positions
c. Increase feed pressure to Train A
d. Increase antiscalant dose to both trains
Back: Answer: b. Verify instrument calibration and check all valve positions

Front:
An RO skid experiences random pressure spikes, and the MF filtrate
flow meter upstream shows occasional negative flow spikes. What is
the most likely cause?
a. Harmonic distortion from the RO feed pump VFD
b. Air entrainment in suction piping or common headers
c. CO₂ stripping in the MF filtrate line
d. SCADA trending or analyzer malfunction
Back: Answer: b. Air entrainment in suction piping or common headers

Front:
RO permeate conductivity rises slightly, but sodium and chloride
remain low while ammonia and neutral organics appear higher in lab
data. What is the best interpretation?
and changing water chemistry
a. Membrane failure with salt passage
b. Analyzer/conductivity reading influenced by non-ionic species
c. Antiscalant breakdown products leaking into permeate
d. Biofilm growth in lead elements
Back: Answer: b. Analyzer/conductivity reading influenced by non-ionic species

Front:
MF flux is lowered to reduce TMP. TMP improves, but the frequency of

explanation?
pressure spikes during integrity tests
a. Lower flux mechanically damages fibers
b. Backwash pressure at lower flux becomes too high
c. Lower flux reduces scouring; solids bridging causes localized
d. Flux must be higher to maintain integrity performance
Back: Answer: c. Lower flux reduces scouring; solids bridging causes localized

Front:
An MF system shows a sudden spike in filtrate turbidity, but TMP
remains stable. What is the most likely issue?
a. A fiber break causing loss of integrity
b. Insufficient air scour during backwash
c. Organic fouling beginning to develop
d. A faulty TMP sensor
Back: Answer: a. A fiber break causing loss of integrity

Front:
An RO train experiences rising differential pressure in the first
stage only. What is the most likely cause? *a. Accumulation of
suspended solids or biological fouling in lead elements
b. Calcium carbonate scaling in the tail elements
c. Membrane compaction
d. Antiscalant overdose
Back: Answer: (not marked)

Front:
A UV reactor shows normal lamp power but decreased UV intensity
readings. What is the likely cause?
a. Quartz sleeve fouling
b. Lamp failure
c. Low UVT
d. Sensor wiring failure
Back: Answer: a. Quartz sleeve fouling

Front:
A plant observes permeate conductivity increasing while permeate
flow remains stable. What is the most probable cause?
a. Membrane damage resulting in reduced salt rejection
b. Low feed pH
c. Reduced RO feed pressure
d. Temperature drop in the feedwater
Back: Answer: a. Membrane damage resulting in reduced salt rejection

Front:
During MF operation, TMP rises rapidly during a single cycle rather
than gradually over days. What does this indicate? *a. A sudden
increase in feed solids loading
b. A membrane fiber break
c. Low backwash frequency
d. Membrane aging
Back: Answer: (not marked)

Front:
In UV AOP, the operator notices a sudden drop in UVT but stable NOM
in upstream monitoring. What could be happening?
a. Organic contamination or chemical breakthrough upstream of UV
b. Lamp aging
c. Low peroxide dose
d. Reduced flow rate
Back: Answer: a. Organic contamination or chemical breakthrough upstream of UV

Front:
An RO system shows reduced recovery while TMP remains stable. What
is the likely cause?
a. Restriction or malfunction of the concentrate control valve
b. Scaling in the tail elements
c. Low feed temperature
d. Membrane compaction
Back: Answer: a. Restriction or malfunction of the concentrate control valve

Front:
During PDT (pressure decay testing), the system fails despite no
visible leaks. What is the most likely cause? *a. A pinhole or
microcrack in the membrane fibers
b. Bad pressure gauge calibration
c. Low feed conductivity
d. Excessive turbidity
Back: Answer: (not marked)

Front:
A UV reactor triggers a low-dose alarm even though lamp intensity is
within range. What could be the reason?
a. Flow rate is too high for validated RED delivery
b. Peroxide dose is too high
c. Temperature is too low
d. Nitrate levels are high
Back: Answer: a. Flow rate is too high for validated RED delivery

Front:
An RO system shows increasing salt passage and decreasing permeate
flow. Which condition is indicated?
a. Membrane degradation or oxidation damage
b. Concentration polarization reduction
c. Low pH scaling
d. Reduced feed alkalinity
Back: Answer: a. Membrane degradation or oxidation damage

Front:
A SCADA trend shows sudden oscillation in RO feed pressure. What is
the most likely cause?
a. A malfunctioning or unstable control valve
b. Loss of membrane integrity
c. Low temperature compensation factor (TCF)
d. Fouling in the concentrate stage
Back: Answer: a. A malfunctioning or unstable control valve

Front:
A GAC contactor used for microconstituent removal shows early
breakthrough. What is the likely reason?
a. High influent organic loading saturating adsorption sites
b. Excessive backwashing frequency
c. Reduced RO rejection upstream
d. High alkalinity
Back: Answer: a. High influent organic loading saturating adsorption sites

Front:
An MF rack repeatedly fails integrity testing after passing earlier
in the day. What could explain this?
a. Temperature or pressure instability during the test
b. Membrane oxidation
c. Incorrect calibration of turbidity meter
d. Low air scour rate
Back: Answer: a. Temperature or pressure instability during the test

Front:
RO permeate flow slowly decreases over several weeks while salt
passage remains unchanged. What is the most likely cause?
a. Organic or particulate fouling
b. Membrane oxidation
c. Loss of integrity
d. Concentrate valve sticking
Back: Answer: a. Organic or particulate fouling

Front:
After a power interruption, a UV system restarts but immediately
generates “lamp strike failure” alarms. What is the likely cause?
a. Insufficient warm-up time or ballast malfunction
b. Quartz sleeve fouling
c. High UVT
d. Excessive peroxide dose
Back: Answer: a. Insufficient warm-up time or ballast malfunction

Front:
A plant observes that MF TMP increases only when operating during
peak daytime hours. What may be occurring?
a. Increased solids loading due to diurnal source water changes
b. Reduced backwash pressure
c. Peroxide carryover from UV
d. Lower feed temperature
Back: Answer: a. Increased solids loading due to diurnal source water changes

Front:
An RO cleaning-in-place (CIP) restores permeate flow only partially.
What does this indicate?
a. Irreversible fouling or membrane compaction
b. Underfeeding of antiscalant
c. Low concentrate pH
d. Excessive feed pressure
Back: Answer: a. Irreversible fouling or membrane compaction

Front:
A UV AOP system shows normal UVT and lamp power, but oxidation
performance is low. What is the likely cause?
a. Underfeeding or overdosing hydrogen peroxide
b. High RO permeate pH
c. Lamp fouling
d. High dissolved oxygen
Back: Answer: a. Underfeeding or overdosing hydrogen peroxide

Front:
A SCADA system alarms for “CCP deviation” upstream of UV AOP. What
is the operator’s required response under Title 22?
reporting and response protocols immediately
a. Investigate, correct the parameter, and follow required
b. Wait for the next shift to respond
c. Silence the alarm if water appears clear
d. Resume normal operation without action
Back: Answer: a. Investigate, correct the parameter, and follow required

Front:
A MF system displays a rapid increase in TMP during a single
filtration cycle. Which operational issue does this most likely
indicate?
a. Gradual fouling over several days.
b. Loss of membrane structural integrity.
c. Sudden particulate breakthrough or excessive solids loading.
d. Underfeeding of upstream coagulant.
Back: Answer: c. Sudden particulate breakthrough or excessive solids loading.

Front:
A sudden increase in MF filtrate turbidity indicates:
a. Scaling inside the permeate piping.
b. Potential membrane integrity failure or fiber break.
c. Decreased feed temperature.
d. Excessive peroxide residual from upstream AOP.
Back: Answer: b. Potential membrane integrity failure or fiber break.

Back: Answer: b. PFAS concentration in the GAC effluent approaching the

Front:
A GAC bed used for removal of trace organic contaminants begins to
release previously adsorbed contaminants. This phenomenon is called:
a. Bed breakthrough.
b. Carbon attrition.
c. Desorption.
d. Regeneration failure.
Back: Answer: c. Desorption.

Front:
A plant observes an unexpected increase in RO permeate conductivity
while permeate flow remains normal. What is the most likely cause?
a. Scaling in the concentrate stage.
b. Membrane surface damage or loss of rejection.
c. Low temperature reducing flux.
d. Concentrate-line backpressure issues.
Back: Answer: b. Membrane surface damage or loss of rejection.

Front:
A plant observes a rapid decrease in RO feed pH without any changes
in chemical feed. What is the most likely cause?
a. Scaling in the tail elements.
b. CO₂ release or absorption imbalance in pretreatment.
c. Excess antiscalant residual.
d. Membrane oxidation.
Back: Answer: b. CO₂ release or absorption imbalance in pretreatment.

Front:
A plant using chloramination identifies an increasing trend of
nitrosamine formation. Which condition most contributes to this?
a. Low ammonia levels.
b. High chlorine-to-ammonia ratio.
c. High organic nitrogen concentration.
d. Low water temperature.
Back: Answer: c. High organic nitrogen concentration.

Front:
A potable reuse AWT facility observes that nitrification is
occurring in the distribution system. Which condition most increases
this risk?
a. Low water age combined with high residuals.
b. Maintaining pH below 6.5.
c. Warm temperatures combined with low chloramine residual.
d. High free chlorine applied at the plant.
Back: Answer: c. Warm temperatures combined with low chloramine residual.

Front:
MF filtrate turbidity increases while TMP remains stable. What does
this most likely indicate?
a. Severe fouling.
b. Possible fiber break or membrane breach.
c. Underfed coagulant.
d. Overdosed chlorine residual.
Back: Answer: b. Possible fiber break or membrane breach.

Front:
A plant’s UV disinfection system shows a significant drop in RED
(Reduction Equivalent Dose). Which operational condition most likely
caused this decrease?
a. Higher lamp power.
b. Increased flow rate.
c. Reduced UVT due to increased organic matter.
d. Lower lamp cooling water temperature.
Back: Answer: c. Reduced UVT due to increased organic matter.

Front:
A plant operating a UV system notes sleeve fouling. This most
directly decreases which parameter?
a. Flow through the reactor.
b. Lamp electrical efficiency.
c. UV intensity delivered to the water.
d. Reactor chamber temperature.
Back: Answer: c. UV intensity delivered to the water.

Front:
A plant operating an MF–RO–UV AOP system sees a sudden decrease in
UVT after RO. What is the most common cause?
a. Lamp aging.
b. Excess peroxide feed.
c. Dissolved organic matter entering the UV stage.
d. Flow decrease.
Back: Answer: c. Dissolved organic matter entering the UV stage.

Front:
A potable reuse facility notes a drop in RO recovery while TMP
remains stable. Which operational issue does this most likely
indicate?
a. Organic fouling.
b. Scaling on the concentrate side.
c. Permeate valve restriction or instrumentation error.
d. Sudden increase in feed TDS.
Back: Answer: c. Permeate valve restriction or instrumentation error.

Front:
A sudden increase in RO feed pressure is required to maintain the
same flux. What is the most likely cause?
a. Scaling in the tail elements.
b. Increased membrane fouling.
c. Membrane compaction.
d. Reduced concentrate backpressure.
Back: Answer: b. Increased membrane fouling.

Front:
During RO operations, normalized permeate flow begins to decline.
What does this most commonly indicate?
a. Membrane oxidation.
b. Early-stage fouling (organic, biological, or colloidal).
c. Temperature increase in the feed.
d. Increased recovery.
Back: Answer: b. Early-stage fouling (organic, biological, or colloidal).

Front:
A potable reuse plant observes an unexpected shift in permeate pH.
Feed pH remains constant. What is the most likely cause?
a. Scaling upstream of the membranes.
b. Crossflow velocity too high.
c. Membrane degradation allowing passage of acidic species.
d. Low disinfectant residual in pretreatment.
Back: Answer: c. Membrane degradation allowing passage of acidic species.
